paragraphs.heading: A rearrangement
paragraphs.text: In mathematics, a permutation is a bijective function that takes a finite set onto itself. If the set is laid out as an ordered sequence, a permutation moves its members to new places: for a permutation f, f(i) is where the ith member ends up. For example, the permutation sending 1, 2, 3, 4 to 1, 3, 2, 4 can be written simply as the sequence (1, 3, 2, 4).

paragraphs.heading: Counting them
paragraphs.text: Anagrams are a familiar case: they are permutations of a sequence of letters. For n distinct objects, the number of permutations is the product of the first n positive integers, called n factorial and written n!. A related idea is the k-permutation, or partial permutation, an ordered sequence of k distinct elements taken from a set. When k is the size of the whole set, these are just its permutations.

paragraphs.heading: Combining permutations
paragraphs.text: Doing one permutation after another is called permutation composition. All the permutations of a set with n elements form a group under composition, the symmetric group Sₙ. For σ and τ in Sₙ, the product π = στ is given by π(i) = σ(τ(i)). Order usually matters: τσ and στ are typically not equal.

paragraphs.heading: Cycles and fixed points
paragraphs.text: Applying a permutation over and over to one element traces out a cycle, and a cycle with k elements is a k-cycle. An element the permutation leaves where it is, so that σ(x) = x, is a fixed point. A permutation with no fixed points at all is a derangement. One that swaps two elements and fixes the rest is a transposition.

paragraphs.heading: Ancient beginnings
paragraphs.text: Objects like permutations, the hexagrams of the I Ching, were used in China as early as 1000 BC. Plutarch reported that Xenocrates of Chalcedon (396–314 BC) worked out how many syllables the Greek language allows, which would be the first recorded attempt at a hard problem in permutations and combinations. Later the Arab mathematician and cryptographer Al-Khalil (717–786) wrote the Book of Cryptographic Messages. The book makes the first use of permutations and combinations, listing every possible Arabic word with and without vowels.

paragraphs.heading: Into algebra
paragraphs.text: Around 1770 Joseph Louis Lagrange noticed that how the roots of a polynomial equation can be permuted is tied to whether the equation can be solved. Through the work of Évariste Galois this led to Galois theory, which fully describes which polynomial equations in one unknown can be solved by radicals. Studying permutations as substitutions on n elements, notably in Cauchy's 1815 memoir, also gave rise to the idea of a group.

paragraphs.heading: Breaking Enigma
paragraphs.text: Permutations helped crack the Enigma machine, the cipher device Nazi Germany used in World War II. The cryptologist Marian Rejewski used the fact that two permutations are conjugate exactly when they share the same cycle type. With it he broke the German cipher around 1932–1933.
